title: Regression on estimated treatment effects
html:
A balanced one-way layout with a treatments and m observations each is analysed, and the estimated effects α^1,…,α^a are reported under the side condition ∑kα^k=0 (@thm-est-side-conditions). A second analyst, with access only to these numbers, regresses them on the dose xk applied to treatment k, fitting E(α^k)=β0+β1xk with an intercept.

The reported vector has 𝛂Cov(α^)=τ2V with V=Ia−11⊤/a and τ2=σ2/m, because α^k=Y¯k−Y¯ and the Y¯k are uncorrelated with variance τ2. Here q=a−1, C(V)=1⊥, and N=1/a. With 1∈C(X) we get d=1 and r=2, so @thm-ggm-singular(b) gives exactly r−d=1 perfectly known function: X⊤N∝(a,∑kxk)⊤, so 𝛃𝛂aβ0+(∑kxk)β1=1⊤Xβ=1⊤α^=0 with probability one. In words: the intercept is determined by the slope, β0=−x¯β1, and the data say so without error. Fitting an intercept was a mistake, and the model itself reveals it.

Everything else is unchanged. Because VX=X−1(1⊤X)/a has columns in C(X), @thm-ggm-ols-blue applies and ordinary least squares is already best: β^1 is the usual centred slope and β^0=−x¯β^1. Since V is idempotent, V+=V and 𝛆𝛆SSEV=ε^⊤ε^ is the usual residual sum of squares, on q−d=a−2 degrees of freedom. What is not unchanged is the covariance matrix. Because 𝛂1⊤α^=0 exactly, Var(β^1)=τ2Sxx,Var(β^0)=x¯2Var(β^1),Cov(β^0,β^1)=−x¯Var(β^1), whereas the ordinary formula s2(X⊤X)−1 reports s2(1/a+x¯2/Sxx) for the intercept. With a=5 doses 0,1,2,4,8, m=6 replicates and σ=1.2, so τ2=0.24, x¯=3.0 and Sxx=40.0: the true variances are 0.00600 for the slope and 0.0540 for the intercept, while the ordinary formula reports 0.1020 on average for the intercept, too large by a factor of 1.89. A simulation of 200,000 layouts reproduces 0.00600 and 0.0540.
